newsitem.title: USA: Democrats challenge fraud claim in La. Senate race.
newsitem.headline: Democrats challenge fraud claim in La. Senate race.

text.p: Democrats Tuesday challenged claims by Republican Senate candidate Louis "Woody" Jenkins of widespread election fraud in his loss last November to Democrat Mary Landrieu in Louisiana.

Landrieu defeated Jenkins by 5,788 votes but Jenkins asked the Senate to nullify the results and order a new election. Landrieu was certified by Louisiana as the winner and sworn in Jan. 7 without prejudice, meaning she still could lose her seat.

"We believe, based on the evidence uncovered, that a large number of voters in Orleans Parish (New Orleans) were transported to the polls and voted multiple times," Jenkins told the Senate Rules Committee at a hearing Tuesday.
"Unfortunately, in my state, political corruption is nothing new," Jenkins added.
Jenkins blamed New Orleans Democratic Mayor Marc Morial and his political organisation for the alleged fraud, rather than Landrieu or her campaign staff. Morial backed Landrieu.
Jenkins trailed Landrieu in New Orleans by about 101,000 votes, but carried the rest of the state by 95,000 votes.
Attorneys for Landrieu, the daughter of former New Orleans Mayor Moon Landrieu, said Jenkins had not presented any legally competent evidence to support his charges.
"All of Mr. Jenkins' allegations have turned out to be false claims," Scott Bickford told the committee.
"I can't find any proof of what you are saying," Democratic Sen. Dianne Feinstein of California, a committee member, told Jenkins.
New Jersey Democrat Robert Torricelli told Jenkins that if he presented the same evidence to a federal court, his case would be thrown out.

Last week, two outside attorneys hired by the committee, one a Democrat and the other a Republican, recommended dismissal of about half of Jenkins' allegations. But they said there was enough evidence to warrant a limited investigation of the remaining fraud charges.
The nine Republicans and seven Democrats on the Rules Committee were scheduled to vote Thursday on whether to continue the investigation or dismiss the allegations.

The full Senate would have to approve any decision for a new election and Democrats would almost certainly try to block such a vote with a filibuster. Republicans have a 55-45 Senate majority, but it takes 60 votes to stop a filibuster.
